description: Somos Cyberbugs, un equipo de estudiantes de Ingeniería en Software y Tecnologías Emergentes e Inteligencia de Negocios de la UABC.
summary:
Little Big Steps Martian Colony is a resource management game for children aged 7 to 12, in which they manage a small base on Mars and make decisions to keep their crew safe. Players assign colonists to tasks and missions, and decide how to allocate available oxygen, water, food, energy, and budget. Every decision comes at a cost: directing energy to the radiation shelter leaves less for the greenhouse—and because of communication delays, supplies, new colonists, and funds from Earth arrive several "sols" (Martian days) late.

The Sun in the game is real: solar flares, coronal mass ejections, particle showers, and geomagnetic storms are drawn from NASA’s space weather database, DONKI. These events appear in the order they actually occurred and are labeled "Real NASA Data," distinguishing the actual historical events from their specific impact on the colony. A guided tutorial, an interactive glossary, and fun facts sourced from NASA turn every decision into a STEM lesson. The game is available in both Spanish and English.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Little Big Steps: Martian Colony puts children aged 7 to 12 in charge of a base on Mars. The game progresses in "sols" (Martian days, each lasting 24.66 hours). During each sol, the colony produces and consumes oxygen (kg), water (L), food (kg), and energy: solar panels generate kW, modules consume kW, and batteries store the surplus in kWh. The player:

  • Builds and connects modules, including life support, a greenhouse, power systems, storage, a drill, a workshop, crew quarters, a radiation shelter, a landing pad, and a Command Module.
  • Assigns colonists to tasks and missions; each colonist has a health status and an accumulated radiation level.
  • Manages storage and the kitchen, including capacity, rationing, and recipes.
  • Requests supplies, additional colonists, and funding from Earth—which arrive several sols later due to the distance (communication delay).
  • Upgrades the Command Module; reaching the maximum level wins the game.

REAL NASA DATA

The solar activity featured is not fictional. The game pulls data from NASA DONKI (CCMC / NASA Goddard), including solar flares (FLR), coronal mass ejections (CME), solar energetic particles (SEP), geomagnetic storms (GST), interplanetary shocks (IPS), high-speed solar wind streams (HSS), magnetopause crossings (MPC), and radiation belt enhancements (RBE). These events occur in the same sequence as they did in reality. Major events—such as X-class flares, fast CMEs, SEPs, or geomagnetic storms with a Kp index ≥ 7—pause the game and present the player with choices that carry different costs (for example, sending the crew to a shielded shelter versus keeping the greenhouse powered). Minor events appear as updates in the mission log. Each real-world event is labeled "NASA REAL-WORLD DATA," including its date, class or speed, and a link to the source. A clear distinction is always maintained between "what actually happened" and "what is occurring within the colony." Data is retrieved in real-time (covering the last 120 days); if no internet connection is available, the system defaults to the most recently saved download or an included dataset (which features the solar storms from May 2024). The source of the data currently in use is always indicated.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Players learn through decision-making rather than passive reading. They experience trade-offs—addressing one need leaves fewer resources for another—gain an understanding of why radiation and communication delays with Earth matter, and connect the gameplay to actual space weather. A guided tutorial explains the mechanics step-by-step, while a glossary of over 30 terms—introduced and highlighted the first time they appear—clarifies the vocabulary. Additionally, interesting facts sourced from NASA, the JPL, and other organizations are presented at relevant moments. The game is suitable for use at home or in the classroom and is available in both Spanish and English.

TOOLS

Godot Engine 4.5 with GDScript; NASA DONKI API (CCMC); Python scripts for downloading DONKI data; Figma for conceptualization and prototyping; Aseprite and Paint Tool SAI for pixel art creation; Canva for presentations; Git/GitHub for version control and collaboration.

CREATIVITY AND CONSIDERATIONS

Instead of relying on generic, randomized "solar storms," ​​the threats presented are actual events recorded by NASA. Designed for ages 7–12, the game features concise text, two-choice decision-making with visible consequences, a pixel-art aesthetic reminiscent of a control console, and real-world units explained within their proper context. The game functions offline—ensuring accessibility for classrooms without internet—and we prioritize data integrity: a clear distinction is always made between the actual event and its simulated effect in the game, with direct links provided for every source.
